To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the aggregate characteristics of American and non-American women with a variety of gynecologic malignancy diagnoses are remarkably similar, except for a few notable differences that are suggestive of a more conservative surgical philosophy among non-American patients.
American and non-American women with cancer are similar in most clinical features but differ with respect to the use of radiotherapy and surgical management of recurrent disease.
the American and non-American patient populations were remarkably similar in clinical characteristics.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of an information retrieval system that is capable of answering the information needs of patients with gynecological cancers.
the development of an Internet-based decision-support tool for patients with ovarian cancer, and the evaluation of its effectiveness in improving patient outcomes.
the clinical characteristics of American versus non-American gynecological cancer patients requesting information about treatment options from a proprietary web based decision-support program.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, in general, American and non-US patients with gynecological cancers have similar clinical characteristics.
, in general, American gynecologic cancer Web site users appear to be similar to their non-American counterparts in terms of clinical characteristics.
American gynecologic cancer survivors and patients seeking information on the Internet are remarkably similar to their international counterparts.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the Internet can be a valuable tool for the delivery of cancer-related information, and that it may be useful for the development and delivery of cancer-related decision-support programs, even when used by non-American populations.
the Internet can be used by non-American gynecology cancer patients as a means of gaining access to US-based cancer information.

the Internet is a powerful tool that can provide access to health information regardless of geographic location, and that this information is being used by patients in the same way across national boundaries.
The main takeaway from our work is that
patients with gynecological cancers, regardless of where they live, want information about treatment options, and are willing to provide personal information about themselves in order to receive it.
the Internet has substantially leveled the playing field in terms of providing health-related information to individuals with gynecologic cancer, regardless of their location.
the Internet can provide a means to deliver health-related information to patients worldwide. © 2007 Wiley-Liss, Inc. Hensley, M. L., K
